newsitem.title: UK: Blair charges up British opposition before poll.
newsitem.headline: Blair charges up British opposition before poll.

text.p: Tony Blair, trying to take Labour into government after 17 years in the wilderness, delivered a rallying call to the British opposition party's conference that appeared to have papered over internal splits.

After weeks of arguments over his views of Labour's links with unions and whether he has pushed his party too far from its socialist roots, Blair had to unite his party on Tuesday for the last push to an election now no more than seven months away.
As delegates left the conference hall in this northern English seaside resort after one of Blair's most personal speeches ever, all the signs were he had succeeded.
"It was inspirational, the speech of the next prime minister of this country," Janet Foster, a party delegate from Wolverhampton in central England, told Reuters.
"I can't wait for the election, I can't wait to show (Prime Minister John) Major."

Even traditional Labour members, many of whom have been dismayed by Blair's eagerness to ditch the party's traditional socialist dogmas and drag it into the political centreground since he took over as leader in 1994, were won over.

"I think the points he went over have covered some of the doubts we've had in recent weeks. I think he's bridged that gap between old and new Labour," veteran Labour member of parliament Sir Ray Powell told Reuters.

"We lost the last election and we had the same feeling that we were going to win. I don't want to run up against the buffers again by alienating too many people. I think this speech will have satisfied most of the doubts," he said.
Labour lost at the last general election in 1992 despite polls predicting it would win.

But Blair has argued consistently that there is no room for complacency despite polls now giving Labour a 20 point plus lead, adding that his drive to modernise the party has been necessary to give it a chance of power.
To do that, he has eased Labour's links with the unions and promised in his speech that "the Labour government is not the political arm of anyone today other than the British people".
The ruling conservatives turned their big guns on Blair's address.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said: "This was one of the most deceitful speeches in British political history. Not a contract with Britain, but a con-trick on Britain."
"It was a nasty, spiteful speech riddled with hypocrisy. Britain's middle classes will not be fooled."
But even Labour leaders who have resisted some of Blair's reforms were enthusiastic on Tuesday.
Bill Morris, leader of the Transport and General Workers' Union, told Reuters: "It was a speech of the times, of the moment. We're ready for government."
A few delegates were concerned about the slick presentation, designed to come across well on news bulletins.
"I think it was typical of the Democratic Conventions in the United States, which is perhaps the way we're going," said Jane Young, another local party delegate.
But a senior Labour aide dismissed suggestions Blair had become too slick. "After all," one said, "the Democrats have been fairly successful."
And 82-year-old Matilda Edelman, a lifelong party member who has been attending annual conferences since 1945, told Reuters: "The conference has never been so united... It was a winning speech."
